# Graham Priest — "The Logic of the Catuskoti" (2010)

## Bibliographic identity

The selected object is Graham Priest, "The Logic of the Catuskoti," *Comparative Philosophy* 1, no. 2 (2010): 24–54, open access at scholarworks.sjsu.edu. Metadata and full text verified against the open-access PDF. Because the article is freely and fully accessible, it is this bank's quotation-ready formal core for Priest's catuṣkoṭi machinery: wherever the essay needs exact wording that the 2018 book house ([[symbolon/episteme/sources/mathematics-logic/priest/priest-2018-fifth-corner/priest-2018-fifth-corner.md|priest-2018-fifth-corner]]) can currently supply only as review transcription, this article supplies it verified. Page numbers below follow the open-access PDF; a spot-check against the journal's own pagination remains open.

## Source scholarship

The article is the compressed original of the 2018 book's formal arc. It opens by taking the catuṣkoṭi at face value: "given any question, there are four possibilities, yes, no, both, and neither" (p. 24). It then states the classical embarrassment exactly — "the four cases are supposed to be exclusive; yet case (c) entails both cases (a) and (b)" (p. 27) — and resolves it by moving to First Degree Entailment, whose four values are the subsets of {T, F} arranged in the diamond lattice: "Negation maps t to f, vice versa, n to itself, and b to itself. Conjunction is greatest lower bound, and disjunction is least upper bound." (p. 33). On this semantics the four corners are exclusive and exhaustive, and the early tetralemma is formally innocent.

The pressure comes from Nāgārjuna's rejection of all four corners. Priest's answer is the fifth status: "They have some other status, namely, (e): none of the above." (pp. 36–37), with the infection conditions e-in/e-out (pp. 37–38) making ineffability spread through any compound that contains it. The self-referential embarrassment of ineffability-talk is met by plurivalence: "evaluations are thought of, not as functions, but as relations, which relate sentences to some number of these values" (p. 44), so a sentence can be related both to a spoken value and to e. The article even turns the catuṣkoṭi on itself — asked whether the koṭis are exclusive, "The correct option in this case is the third: they are and are not" (pp. 42–43) — a dialetheic self-application the essay reads as the value-theory straining toward what it cannot write. At the two-truths level the formalism reaches its own silence: at the ultimate level "nothing of the form Tu⟨A⟩, Fu⟨A⟩, or Bu⟨A⟩ can hold; only things of the form Nu⟨A⟩ — or perhaps more appropriately, Eu⟨A⟩" (p. 47). Priest closes by placing the construction historically: "The catuskoti and its ramifications are a central part of logic in both the original and the later Madhyamaka Buddhist traditions" (p. 48).

## Essay use

### Source's relevant contribution

The verified formal statements of the four-corner FDE semantics, the fifth status e with its infection conditions, plurivalent evaluation, the self-application of the tetralemma, and the ultimate-level silence — the exact wording the essay's §3 formal reconstruction quotes.

### Licensed essay use

- Quote the formal machinery verbatim in [[28-s3-p3-projective-dimensional-reframing]] as the codification of QL's four explicit positions and the arrival at the ground.
- Use q007 (only Eu⟨A⟩ at the ultimate level) as the formalism's own falling-silent — the point where the return must be performed rather than written.
- Use q008 for the historical standing of the catuṣkoṭi in Madhyamaka logic.

### Claim boundary

This is Priest's construction, not settled history of the catuṣkoṭi. The reception gates recorded in [[symbolon/episteme/sources/mathematics-logic/priest/priest-2018-fifth-corner/priest-2018-fifth-corner.md|priest-2018-fifth-corner]] (Siderits, Westerhoff, Green, Kapsner) apply to this article's machinery equally and must be cross-referenced wherever it is used. The reading of e's arrival as arrival at QL's #0 — and of the tradition as performing the 5→0 return — is the essay's own Argued move, not Priest's.
